blocks.text: On a foggy night in Low Marrow, the river ran black beneath the trees. A villager stepped from the muddy bank into the wooden ferryboat, shivering as his boots hit the floorboards. He carried no coin purse, only a heavy posture and eyes wet with regret.
The Ferryman stood silent at the bow in his wide-brimmed hat, wrapped in a long grey oilskin coat. He extended one weathered hand without speaking.

The villager bent close to the bow lantern and whispered the dark night he had struck his own brother. The Ferryman closed his fingers over the spoken breath. When he opened his palm, the secret had hardened into a smooth pale stone, heavy as river silt.
He laid the stone gently into the bottom of the hull. The villager blinked, wiped his brow, and looked around as if waking from sleep.

His shoulders dropped, the bitter anger vanished from his face, and he stared toward the market shore, unable to recall why he had wept. "Step across," the Ferryman said quietly. Once, in Low Marrow, the ferry cost one memory.
Three dawns later, morning mist hung thick over the river. The Fisherman boarded the ferry, a heavy coil of rope slung over his shoulder and a dark wool cap pulled low.

He twisted the frayed fibers of the rope in his hands, trembling as he stared into the swirling currents. Months had passed since the spring flood, yet every time he closed his eyes, he heard the timber beams of his cottage snapping against the wall of water.
He could still see his nets tearing in the mud, his livestock drowning in the dark. The Ferryman lifted his hand, holding his broad palm steady beneath the rising sun.
The Fisherman leaned down and breathed the terror of that night into the old man's grip—the roaring water, the screaming wind, the loss of everything he owned.

The Ferryman closed his fingers tight. When he opened them, a second smooth pale stone rested in his hand. He placed it beside the first on the timber floorboards of the hull. The Fisherman exhaled deeply.

He smoothed his cap, slung his rope higher, and looked out across the quiet grey water. The memory was gone. He no longer remembered why he had ever feared the river's mudbank, or why he had wept upon the shore.

He smiled, unburdened and light. Word of the painless ferry spread through the cottages of Low Marrow. Before long, villagers arrived at the riverbank every day to trade away their shame, debts, and broken promises.

The Mayor crossed most often of all. Stout and ruddy-faced, he wore a bright crimson sash and a heavy brass chain of office. He stepped onto the ferry boat every week, flushed with temper from fierce town council disputes or public embarrassments.
He reached habitually for his coin purse before remembering the fare. Leaning over the Ferryman's open palm, the Mayor whispered away the memory of his bad decisions and sharp words.

The Ferryman closed his hand, produced another pale river stone, and set it carefully alongside the others. Immediately, the Mayor’s scowl vanished. He adjusted his brass chain, crossed his arms proudly over his sash, and laughed with unearned confidence as the boat drifted toward the market shore.
The villagers grew light and kind, greeting each other with cheerful smiles in the muddy streets.

But with each crossing, the Ferryman’s boat sat lower in the water. The dark river line crept higher along the outer wooden planks, weighed down by the growing pile of pale stones resting inside the hull.

Two months passed, bringing clear dawn light over the low banks of Low Marrow. From the middle of the river, the Ferryman rested his heavy oars and watched the shore. On the flat mudbank right at the water’s edge, the young Fisherman was hard at work.

He whistled a bright tune, driving thick timber posts into the dark silt with heavy iron blows. Slung over his shoulder was the same coil of frayed rope he always carried, but his face held no shadow of past terror.
The Ferryman recognized the exact patch of ground. Only two springs ago, the rising river had torn through this low bank, splintering the Fisherman’s cottage and sweeping his possessions downstream.
The Fisherman had stood on the shore then, weeping for everything he had lost. Now, unburdened by the memory of that terrible thaw, the young man hammered his new foundations into the soft silt.
He smiled at the cool water lapping against his boots, unaware that he was building his home directly in the path of the next flood.

Without the weight of past disaster to guide his hands, he walked joyfully back into the very danger that had once destroyed him. By noon the following day, the Mayor stood on the muddy bank beside two ancient, moss-covered stone piers.

Dark water swirled around the ruined masonry, all that remained of the old bridge that had collapsed long ago. Adjusting his heavy brass chain over his crimson sash, the Mayor gestured grandly toward the opposite shore.

He announced a plan to construct a magnificent new stone bridge directly upon those broken piers, reconnecting the trade routes once and for all. The Ferryman pulled his wooden boat to the landing and stepped onto the mud.

He looked at the cracked stone, then spoke directly to the civic leader. "The riverbed beneath those piers is soft sand," the Ferryman said. "When the spring tides rise, the current undercuts the foundation.
That is why the old bridge cracked and fell." The Mayor’s cheerful expression faltered. A sudden wave of irritation and sharp anxiety tightened his chest.

The Ferryman’s words stirred an uncomfortable doubt he did not wish to bear. The Mayor stared at the piers, his pride wounded by the sudden threat of failure. Refusing to let caution derail his grand project, the Mayor turned away from the river and eyed the Ferryman's waiting boat.
Late that afternoon, as the sun dipped behind the timber cottages, the Mayor stepped onto the wooden ferry. He could not endure the lingering worry that the new bridge might collapse.
Leaning close to the Ferryman’s stooped shoulder, the Mayor cupped his hands and whispered the warning he had just received into the Ferryman’s open palm.

He handed over the memory of the soft riverbed, the crumbling sand, and the Ferryman’s grave words. The Ferryman closed his dark fingers around the spoken secret. When he opened his hand, a smooth pale stone rested in his palm.
He laid the stone carefully into the bottom of the hull alongside the dozens already gathered there. With a deep breath, the Mayor stood tall. The anxious crease on his brow vanished entirely.
He adjusted his brass chain, smiled at the distant shoreline, and forgot that anyone had ever spoken of danger. The Ferryman watched the Mayor step onto the far bank with unburdened confidence.

But inside the hull, the new stone pressed down with sudden weight. The wooden boat settled deeper into the river, its upper rim floating mere inches above the dark, silent water. Dusk settled over the grey river as workers laid the final arch of the new stone bridge directly upon the ancient, cracked piers.
Standing at the water’s edge, the Ferryman looked up at the structure, then turned to the Mayor.

For the first time, the Ferryman broke his silence. He described how sixty winters ago, heavy rains had scoured the sandy riverbed, causing those exact piers to tilt and crumble beneath the masonry. He spoke of the families who had wept, the ruined trade, and the hard lessons the village had once pledged never to abandon.
He explained that in surrendering their grief to his boat, they had not merely discarded their pain; they had given away every reason they possessed for caution.
The Mayor listened politely, a soft smile resting on his face. He smoothed down his crimson sash, then held out an open palm over the ferry’s rim.

"And what would it cost to forget this too?" The Ferryman stared down at the outstretched hand. He realized the quiet terror of his trade: any truth he offered would only be returned to him as another fare.
Without a word, he closed his fingers over the Mayor’s secret, placing the fresh stone into the crowded hull. When the spring thaw arrived, the mountains shed their winter snow into swollen torrents.
A massive surge of water rushed down the valley, battering the stone piers. Just as before, the soft sand beneath the riverbed washed away in the heavy current.

Without solid ground below, the ancient stone piers cracked under the pressure. The new bridge buckled, its fresh masonry splitting down the middle before plunging into the foam. Downstream, the rising river swept across the mudbank, carrying off the Fisherman’s timber hut as though it were driftwood.
At the ferry landing, the wooden boat churned against its mooring post. Hundreds of pale stones sat packed inside the hull, dragging the wooden rim level with the river.

A wave broke over the stern. Weighted down by forgotten quarrels, debts, and erased warnings, the boat filled rapidly. The rope tether snapped. Slowly, the ferry sank to the silted riverbed, its cargo scattering across the submerged rocks.
No lives were lost in the sudden surge. At dawn, the river quieted into placid water. The townspeople gathered on the bank, staring in bewilderment at the empty sky where their structure had stood.
The Mayor stroked his chain of office, gazing out across the water and shaking his head at the ruined piers. "Who would build a bridge there?"

The Ferryman looked down through the clear water at the pale stones resting quietly on the riverbed. He recognized every discarded secret scattered across the silt. Without speaking, he retrieved his broadaxe and began shaping fresh timber for a new boat.
Before the first frame was set, a villager stepped forward and held out an open palm. "What does it cost?" In Low Marrow, the river remembers everything.
The people only remember the price.
